claims.text: Adding 1–5 at.% of a refractory microalloying element such as W or Ta to a high-entropy alloy will form nanoscale precipitates.
The precipitates produced by the refractory addition will remain thermally stable at elevated temperatures.
The nanoscale precipitates will hinder dislocation motion.
The nanoscale precipitates will impede grain-boundary sliding.
The refractory element will promote precipitation hardening by precipitating as stable high-temperature phases.
Obstruction of dislocation pathways by the precipitates will mitigate creep deformation during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
The refractory-added alloy will have higher elevated-temperature yield strength than the unmodified alloy under identical test conditions.
The refractory-added alloy will have greater creep resistance than the unmodified alloy under identical test conditions.
The proposed improvement is expected under sustained mechanical load at approximately 800–1000 °C.
The intervention is applicable to aggressive extreme-environment settings such as aerospace or nuclear service.
At substantially lower temperatures or under different loading regimes, the beneficial effect may not occur.
Precipitation hardening is a well-established mechanism in many alloy systems.
The magnitude of improvement will depend on overall alloy composition, processing history, and the refractory element selected.
